problems.objective: Prove that a divisor of the group order need not occur as a subgroup order.
problems.statement: Prove $A_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$, even though $6\mid12$. Conclude the converse of Lagrange's theorem is false.

$A_4$ has eight $3$-cycles, which form conjugacy classes of size $4$ inside $A_4$.

problems.solution: If $|H|=6$, then $[A_4:H]=2$, so $H$ is normal. The conjugacy classes of $A_4$ have sizes $1$ for the identity, $3$ for the double transpositions, and $4,4$ for the two classes of $3$-cycles. A normal subgroup is a union of conjugacy classes and contains the identity. No sum beginning with $1$ and using some of $3,4,4$ equals $6$: the possibilities start $1,4,5,8,9,12$. problems.title: A structure test for groups of order six
problems.objective: Use element orders and index to separate the cyclic and nonabelian cases.
problems.statement: Let $G$ have order $6$. Assume $G$ contains an element $a$ of order $3$ and an element $b$ of order $2$. Prove $\langle a\rangle$ is normal. Show that if $ab=ba$, then $G$ is cyclic, while if $ab\ne ba$, the six elements have unique normal forms $e,a,a^2,b,ba,ba^2$ and satisfy $bab^{-1}=a^{-1}$.
permittedResults: A subgroup of index $2$ is normal.
An automorphism of a cyclic group of order $3$ sends a generator to $a$ or $a^{-1}$.
problems.strategy: First: $\langle a\rangle$ has order $3$ and index $2$. Next: If $a,b$ commute, compute the order of $ab$ using coprime orders. Finally: Otherwise conjugation by $b$ cannot fix $a$, so it sends $a$ to $a^{-1}$; then use the two cosets of $\langle a\rangle$.
hints: $\langle a\rangle$ has order $3$ and index $2$.
If $a,b$ commute, compute the order of $ab$ using coprime orders.
Otherwise conjugation by $b$ cannot fix $a$, so it sends $a$ to $a^{-1}$; then use the two cosets of $\langle a\rangle$.
problems.solution: $A=\langle a\rangle$ has order $3$ and index $2$, so it is normal. If $a$ and $b$ commute, their coprime orders give $\operatorname{ord}(ab)=6$, hence $G=\langle ab\rangle$ is cyclic. Otherwise, conjugation by $b$ restricts to a nontrivial automorphism of $A$. The only options send $a$ to $a$ or $a^{-1}$, and the first would mean commutation, so $bab^{-1}=a^{-1}$. The two left cosets are $A=\{e,a,a^2\}$ and $bA=\{b,ba,ba^2\}$; they are disjoint and contain all six elements, giving the unique normal forms.

problems.title: Counting a product set of finite subgroups
problems.objective: Derive the formula $|HK|=|H||K|/|H\cap K|$ without assuming $HK$ is a subgroup.
problems.statement: Let $H,K$ be finite subgroups of $G$. Prove $|HK|=|H||K|/|H\cap K|$ for the set $HK=\{hk:h\in H,k\in K\}$. Do not assume $HK$ is a subgroup.
permittedResults: A surjection from a finite set may be counted by equal-sized fibers.
Subgroups are closed under products and inverses.
problems.strategy: First: Use the surjection $f:H\times K\to HK$ given by $f(h,k)=hk$. Next: Solve $hk=h'k'$ as $h'^{-1}h=k'k^{-1}\in H\cap K$. Finally: Parametrize the fiber over $hk$ by $x\in H\cap K$ using $(hx,x^{-1}k)$.
hints: Use the surjection $f:H\times K\to HK$ given by $f(h,k)=hk$.
Solve $hk=h'k'$ as $h'^{-1}h=k'k^{-1}\in H\cap K$.
Parametrize the fiber over $hk$ by $x\in H\cap K$ using $(hx,x^{-1}k)$.
problems.solution: The map $f(h,k)=hk$ is onto $HK$. Fix $hk\in HK$. For every $x\in H\cap K$, the pair $(hx,x^{-1}k)$ lies in $H\times K$ and maps to $hk$. Conversely, if $h'k'=hk$, then $h^{-1}h'=kk'^{-1}$ lies in $H\cap K$; writing this element as $x$ recovers the pair uniquely as $(hx,x^{-1}k)$. Thus every fiber has exactly $|H\cap K|$ elements. Since $|H\times K|=|H||K|$, equal-fiber counting gives $|H||K|=|HK||H\cap K|$, hence the formula. No closure of $HK$ under multiplication was used.
